story: According to Muisca religion, the goddess Bachué—whose name in the Chibcha language means "the one with the naked breast"—was a mother goddess and the mother of humanity. She emerged from the waters of Iguaque Lake carrying a baby in her arms. This child grew up to become her husband, and together they populated the Earth. She was worshipped in a temple located in what is now the municipality of Chíquiza, an area formerly called "San Pedro de Iguaque." According to the legend, after Bachué accomplished her goal of giving birth to humanity, she and her husband, the parrot god, transformed into snakes and returned to the sacred lagoon from which she had first emerged. The story of Bachué was recorded by the Spanish chronicler Pedro Simón in his book Noticias Historiales. He wrote that the indigenous people also called her "Furachogua," a Chibcha term meaning "the good woman," and that they worshipped her as one of their principal deities. Simón further noted that the Muisca believed Bachué would sometimes return from the underworld to guide her people.
